{{Short description|Numerical analysis method}}
In [[numerical analysis]], the '''fictitious domain method (FD)''' is a numerical technique designed to solve [[partial differential equation]]s on complex geometries by embedding the physical domain into a larger and simpler computational domain. The method consists of extending the equations beyond the physical boundaries and enforcing the interface conditions through a [[Lagrange multiplier|distributed Lagrange multiplier]] in order to recover the correct solution within the original [[Domain of a function|domain]] of interest.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Glowinski |first1=Roland |last2=Pan |first2=Tsorng-Whay |last3=Periaux |first3=Jacques |date=1994-01-01 |title=A fictitious domain method for Dirichlet problem and applications |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0045-7825%2894%2990135-X |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |volume=111 |issue=3 |pages=283–303 |doi=10.1016/0045-7825(94)90135-X |bibcode=1994CMAME.111..283G |issn=0045-7825|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
[[File:Fitted mesh.png|thumb|Example of a fitted mesh for a circular obstacle]]
[[File:Unfitted mesh-overlapping domains.png|thumb|Example of a background unfitted mesh with an overlapping circular obstacle]]
This method belongs to the more general family of unfitted methods (also known as embedded or immersed), which allow solving [[Boundary value problem|interface problems]] on complex or evolving domains without generating a mesh that conforms to the domain’s boundaries.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Geometrically Unfitted Finite Element Methods and Applications |series=Lecture Notes in Computational Science and Engineering |date=2017 |editor-last=Bordas |editor-first=Stéphane P. A. |editor2-last=Burman |editor2-first=Erik |editor3-last=Larson |editor3-first=Mats G. |editor4-last=Olshanskii |editor4-first=Maxim A.   |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-71431-8  |volume=121 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-71431-8 |isbn=978-3-319-71430-1 |issn=1439-7358|url-access=subscription }}</ref> For this reason, the construction of two independent [[Polygon mesh|meshes]] is considered in the fictitious domain method: one for the unfitted background domain and another overlapping mesh that conforms to the interface, but which can move freely during the simulation. As with the [[immersed boundary method]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mittal |first1=Rajat |last2=Iaccarino |first2=Gianluca |date=2005-01-21 |title=Immersed Boundary Methods |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev.fluid.37.061903.175743 |journal=Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics |language=en |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=239–261 |doi=10.1146/annurev.fluid.37.061903.175743 |bibcode=2005AnRFM..37..239M |issn=0066-4189|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and the [[level-set method]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gibou |first1=Frederic |last2=Fedkiw |first2=Ronald |last3=Osher |first3=Stanley |date=2018-01-15 |title=A review of level-set methods and some recent applications |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021999117307441 |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |volume=353 |pages=82–109 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2017.10.006 |bibcode=2018JCoPh.353...82G |osti=1562769 |issn=0021-9991}}</ref> the fictitious domain method is particularly effective for problems with evolving geometries since there is no need to rebuild the mesh but just to move the overlapping one.<ref name=":3" />

The [[Dirichlet boundary condition]]s on immersed closed interfaces are imposed weakly<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Kaizhou |last2=Augarde |first2=Charles E. |last3=Coombs |first3=William M. |last4=Hu |first4=Zhendong |date=2019-05-01 |title=Weak impositions of Dirichlet boundary conditions in solid mechanics: A critique of current approaches and extension to partially prescribed boundaries |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S004578251930060X |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |volume=348 |pages=632–659 |doi=10.1016/j.cma.2019.01.035 |bibcode=2019CMAME.348..632L |issn=0045-7825}}</ref> by the introduction of the distributed Lagrange multiplier which enforces the boundary condition over the whole overlapping region.<ref name=":2" />

A particular application of the fictitious domain method is in [[fluid–structure interaction]] (FSI) problems, where a fluid and an immersed solid interact one each other, exchanging forces through the interface.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | last1=Boffi | first1=Daniele | last2=Gastaldi | first2=Lucia | title=A fictitious domain approach with Lagrange multiplier for fluid-structure interactions | journal=Numerische Mathematik | date=2017 | volume=135 | issue=3 | pages=711–732 | doi=10.1007/s00211-016-0814-1 | arxiv=1510.06856 }}</ref> In this context, the solid is considered to be embedded within the [[computational fluid dynamics]] domain and the coupling conditions at the interface are enforced weakly over the whole fictitious fluid region.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Yu |first=Zhaosheng |date=2005-07-20 |title=A DLM/FD method for fluid/flexible-body interactions |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021999105000148 |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |volume=207 |issue=1 |pages=1–27 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2004.12.026 |bibcode=2005JCoPh.207....1Y |issn=0021-9991|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Weak imposition of Dirichlet boundary conditions ==
Let <math>\Omega_f \subset \mathbb{R}^d </math> be a fluid domain in which we want to solve the [[Stokes flow|Stokes equation]] for [[Newtonian fluid|incompressible Newtonian fluids]]. We want to impose the [[Dirichlet boundary condition]] <math>\textbf{u} = \textbf{g}</math> on the boundary of an immersed circle described by the interface <math>\Gamma = \partial \Omega_{c}</math>. In this context, the fictitious domain method allows us to solve the Stokes equation over the whole domain <math>\Omega = \Omega_f \cup \Omega_{c} </math>, and to impose weakly the constraint <math>\textbf{u} = \textbf{g}</math> by means of the [[Lagrange multiplier]] <math>\mathbf{\lambda}</math>.
[[File:Fictitious domain method simulation.png|thumb|371x371px|Velocity field around a fixed circular obstacle]]
The fictitious domain [[weak formulation]] reads:<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Bertrand |first1=F. |last2=Tanguy |first2=P. A. |last3=Thibault |first3=F. |date=1997 |title=A three-dimensional fictitious domain method for incompressible fluid flow problems |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-0363%2819970930%2925%3A6%3C719%3A%3AAID-FLD585%3E3.0.CO%3B2-K |journal=International Journal for Numerical Methods in Fluids |language=en |volume=25 |issue=6 |pages=719–736 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1097-0363(19970930)25:6<719::AID-FLD585>3.0.CO;2-K |bibcode=1997IJNMF..25..719B |issn=1097-0363|url-access=subscription }}</ref><math display="block">
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \int_{\Omega} \mu \nabla \textbf{u} : \nabla\textbf{v} - \int_{\Omega} p \nabla \cdot \textbf{v} + \langle \mathbf{\lambda} , \textbf{v} \rangle_{\Omega_{c}} = 0 \quad &\forall \textbf{v} \in H^1_0(\Omega)  \\[1ex]
\displaystyle \int_{\Omega} q \ \nabla \cdot \textbf{u}_f = 0 \quad &\forall q \in L^2_0(\Omega) \\[1ex]
\displaystyle \langle \textbf{u} - \textbf{g} , \mathbf{\eta} \rangle_{\Omega_{c}} = 0 \quad &\forall \mathbf{\eta} \in \Lambda
\end{cases}
</math>

The last equation of the system guarantees that, in a weak sense, the interface condition <math>\textbf{u} = \textbf{g}</math> is satisfied over the whole domain <math>\Omega_{c}</math>, and in particular on the interface <math>\Gamma</math>, while in <math>\Omega_f </math> the equation is left untouched.<ref name=":4" />

The Lagrange multiplier <math>\mathbf{\lambda} </math> acts on the fluid as an external force defined only in <math>\Omega_{c} </math> that enforces the fictitious fluid velocity <math>\textbf{u} </math> to fulfil the constraint inside the circle.<ref name=":5" />

== Fluid-structure interaction application ==

As it is typically done in [[Fluid–structure interaction|fluid-structure interaction problems]], we consider a fluid domain <math>\Omega_f \subset \mathbb{R}^d </math>, where the [[Navier–Stokes equations]] are usually solved, and <math>\mathcal{B} \subset \mathbb{R}^d </math> representing the region occupied by the structure.<ref name=":0" /> The fluid is described in an [[Eulerian Coordinates|Eulerian framework]] while the solid is described in a [[Lagrangian coordinates|Lagrangian formulation]]. This means that the solid domain <math>\mathcal{B} </math> can be expressed as the image of a fixed reference configuration <math>\mathcal{B}^* </math> through the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian map]] <math>
x = \text{X}(s,t)
</math>.<ref name=":0" />

The solid structure interacts with the fluid through its interface <math>\Gamma = \partial \mathcal{B}</math>, and from the mathematical point of view, it is required that the following kinematic condition is satisfied at the interface <math>\Gamma
</math>:<math display="block">
\textbf{u}(x,t) = \dfrac{\partial \text{X}(s,t)}{\partial t} \Big|_{x = \text{X}(s,t)}
</math>where <math>\textbf{u}
</math> is the fluid velocity and <math>
x = \text{X}(s,t)
</math> is the position of the Lagrangian coordinate <math>
s
</math> at time <math>
t
</math>. The latter kinematic condition can be seen as a specific [[Dirichlet boundary condition]] at the interface <math>\Gamma</math> which involves both the unknowns <math>\textbf{u}
</math> and <math>
\text{X}
</math> of the problem.<ref name=":0" />

Therefore, in the spirit of the fictitious domain method, we can extend the fluid equation to the whole fixed computational domain <math>\Omega = \Omega_f \cup \mathcal{B} </math> and impose weakly the kinematic coupling condition through the Lagrange multiplier <math>\mathbf{\lambda}</math>, requiring that the fictitious velocity <math>\textbf{u}
</math> matches the time derivative of the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian map]] <math>
\text{X}
</math> in a weak sense inside the solid domain <math>\mathcal{B} </math>.'''<ref name=":0" />'''  
[[File:ADINA R & D FSI Heart Valve Analysis.gif|thumb|319x319px|Numerical simulation of a heart valve]]
This requirement leads to the following [[weak formulation]]:'''<ref name=":0" />'''<math display="block">

\begin{cases}
a_f(\textbf{u}, \textbf{v}) - b(p,\textbf{v}) + \displaystyle \langle \mathbf{\lambda} , \textbf{v}(\text{X}) \rangle_{\mathcal{B}^*} = F_f(\textbf{v}) \quad &\forall \textbf{v} \in H^1_0(\Omega)  \\[1ex]
b(q,\textbf{u})= 0 \quad &\forall q \in L^2_0(\Omega) \\[1ex]
a_s(\text{X}, \text{Y}) - \displaystyle \langle \mathbf{\lambda} , \text{Y} \rangle_{\mathcal{B}^*} = F_s(\text{Y}) \quad &\forall \text{Y} \in H^1(\mathcal{B^*})  \\[1ex]
\displaystyle \langle \textbf{u}(\text{X}) - \dfrac{\partial \text{X}}{\partial t}  , \mathbf{\eta} \rangle_{\mathcal{B}^*} = 0 \quad &\forall \mathbf{\eta} \in \Lambda
\end{cases}

</math>

where <math>a_f(\cdot,\cdot)
</math> and <math>b(\cdot,\cdot)
</math> are the classical [[bilinear form]]s coming from the [[Navier–Stokes equations]], while <math>a_s(\cdot,\cdot)
</math> is the bilinear form associated with the [[Solid mechanics|elastic model]] describing the solid.'''<ref name=":0" />'''

The kinematic condition is represented in a weak sense by the last equation, and the Lagrange multiplier <math>\mathbf{\lambda}</math> acts as a body force on both the fluid and solid equations in order to fulfil this condition.<ref name=":5" />

== Numerical aspects ==
The fictitious domain method proves to be effective for the numerical simulation of moving obstacles, as it employs two independent [[Polygon mesh|meshes]]: a fixed background grid and an independent, overlapping mesh that describes the obstacle geometry.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Boffi |first1=Daniele |last2=Cavallini |first2=Nicola |last3=Gastaldi |first3=Lucia |date=2015-03-04 |title=The Finite Element Immersed Boundary Method with Distributed Lagrange Multiplier |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/140978399 |journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis |language=en |volume=53 |issue=6 |pages=2584–2604 |doi=10.1137/140978399 |issn=0036-1429|url-access=subscription }}</ref> As we have seen in the previous applications, in order to weakly enforce the interface condition, we have to compute the [[duality pairing]] <math display="inline">\displaystyle \langle \mathbf{\lambda} , \textbf{v}\rangle_{\Omega_{ob}}</math> over the obstacle domain <math display="inline">\Omega_{ob}</math>.'''<ref name=":0" />'''<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

The [[Lagrange multiplier]] <math>\mathbf{\lambda}</math> is defined over <math display="inline">\Omega_{ob}</math> while the [[Distribution (mathematics)|test function]] <math>\mathbf{v}</math> is defined over the whole computational domain <math>\Omega</math>. Therefore, upon [[finite element method]] [[discretization]], the discrete Lagrange multiplier <math>\mathbf{\lambda}_h
</math> is defined on the overlapping mesh, whereas the discrete test function <math>\mathbf{v}_h</math> lives on the background mesh.<ref name=":1" /> As a result, computing the above coupling term requires the evaluation of [[basis function]]s defined on the background mesh at locations that belong to the overlapping mesh, which may be change over time. This task is computationally non-trivial and may introduce [[numerical error]]s and possibly wrong solutions.'''<ref name=":1">{{cite arXiv | last1=Boffi | first1=Daniele | last2=Credali | first2=Fabio | last3=Gastaldi | first3=Lucia | title=Quadrature error estimates on non-matching grids in a fictitious domain framework for fluid-structure interaction problems | date=2024 | class=math.NA | eprint=2406.03981 }}</ref>'''

This issue can be handled with different strategies:<ref name=":7">{{cite journal | last1=Boffi | first1=Daniele | last2=Credali | first2=Fabio | last3=Gastaldi | first3=Lucia | title=On the interface matrix for fluid–structure interaction problems with fictitious domain approach | journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering | date=2022 | volume=401 | article-number=115650 | doi=10.1016/j.cma.2022.115650 | arxiv=2205.13350 }}</ref>

* Augmented [[Numerical integration|quadrature rule]]: sub-triangulate the overlapping region in order to adopt an enhanced quadrature formula capable of accurately computing the coupling term. While exact, this approach can be computationally expensive.<ref name=":7" />
* Inexact [[Numerical integration|quadrature rule]]: maintain the original quadrature used for the overlapping mesh, accepting a quadrature error that is controlled by the mesh size <math>h
</math>.<ref name=":1" />
* [[Collocation method]]: project <math>\mathbf{\lambda}_h
</math> over the discrete space of <math>\mathbf{v}_h</math> in order to have both the functions defined on the same mesh.<ref name=":5" />
